jyotis.why_not: Grammatical stem form; Americans read it as 'Joe-tiss' and it sounds like a surname or medical term

shabda.name: Shabda
shabda.say_note: Two clean syllables, no aspirates for an American reader; 'sh' start is intuitive
shabda.collisions: Known as a philosophical term (shabda = word/sound) but very rarely used as a given name

veda.why_not: Widely used as a girl's name in India and the West, and far too well known a word

svana.why_not: The sv- cluster gets mangled and the -ana ending reads feminine (like Svana/Svetlana)

mihira.name: Mihira

mihira.collisions: The short form Mihir is somewhat common among Indian men; the fuller Mihira (as in Varahamihira) is rare
mihira.note: Only use if the family is happy being asked whether it is 'Mihir'

agra.why_not: Reads immediately as the Indian city Agra, and looks like English 'agro'

jnanin.why_not: The jn- cluster is unpronounceable for Americans

dyumat.why_not: Grammatical adjective stem; the dy- cluster and final -mat will be mangled

atapat.why_not: A present participle, not a name; sounds clumsy and repetitive in English

gramani.why_not: Reads as 'grammar-y' to Americans and the meaning (village headman) is a title, not a personal name

jahnu.name: Jahnu

jahnu.note: Distinctive and clearly masculine in origin, with a Ganga connection the family can explain

pravira.name: Pravir
pravira.meaning: a foremost hero, chief among the brave
pravira.say_note: Two syllables, stress obvious, no problem sounds; final -a dropped as is normal in Indian usage
pravira.collisions: Veer/Vir are common, but Pravir is rare and not an older-generation staple
pravira.note: Strong, easy, unmistakably masculine; Pravir Gawande scans well

marisha.why_not: Reads exactly like the girls' name Marisa/Marissa

lakacha.why_not: Means a sticky breadfruit tree; trivial, unattractive meaning

shimbala.why_not: Means a small pod; weak meaning and sounds like nonsense in English

shripati.why_not: A classic older-generation name for men born 1950-1995 and a Vishnu epithet

heti.why_not: Name of a rakshasa king; negative association and sounds feminine

dipta.why_not: Reads as Deepta, used for girls, and Americans will say 'DIP-ta'

nripa.why_not: The nr- cluster is unpronounceable for Americans ('nip-ra'/'nerp-uh')

netra.why_not: Used as a girl's name in India and mainly understood as 'eye'

padma.why_not: Overwhelmingly a feminine name in modern usage

prauna.why_not: Obscure lexical word; the 'au' spelling invites mispronunciation ('prawn-a')

mani.why_not: Reads as English 'money' and is also a common South Indian name/nickname

mantra.why_not: Reads as the ordinary English word 'mantra'

mira.why_not: Established girl's name in both India and the USA

rukma.name: Rukma
rukma.meaning: that which shines; radiant gold, a golden ornament
rukma.say_note: Simple k-m cluster Americans handle easily; no aspirates or retroflexes
rukma.collisions: Rukmini (feminine) is known; masculine Rukma is essentially unused today
rukma.note: Vedic word for radiant gold; masculine in Sanskrit and distinctive in the USA

rucha.why_not: Rucha is a common Marathi girl's name

valgu.why_not: Sounds harsh and odd in English (vulgar/Valgus, a medical term)

vidvas.why_not: Grammatical stem ending in -s; clumsy and unpronounceable as a name

vira.why_not: Too close to the very common Veer/Vir, and reads as the feminine Vera in the USA

shishu.why_not: Means 'infant'; a baby word that would be absurd on an adult

shuchi.why_not: Suchi/Shuchi is used as a girl's name in India

surin.name: Surin
surin.say_note: Reads correctly on first sight; consonant-light and easy to spell back
surin.collisions: Similar in shape to Suresh/Surya but not confusable; also a Thai place name, a minor issue
surin.note: Clean, modern-sounding, and very rare among Indian-American boys

hesha.why_not: Obscure Vedic adjective; reads feminine and sounds like 'Heather/Aisha' blends

urjita.name: Urjit
urjita.meaning: endowed with strength and vigour; mighty, excellent
urjita.say_note: Final -a dropped as in normal Indian usage; 'Ur-jit' is read correctly by Americans
urjita.collisions: Rare but does exist as a name (e.g. Urjit Patel); not common among children
urjita.note: Shares the root urja (energy) which the family can explain easily

jalada.name: Jalad
jalada.say_note: Simple open syllables; final -a dropped so it does not read feminine
jalada.collisions: Close in sound to the common Jalaj/Jalad variants but very rarely used
jalada.note: Nice monsoon imagery with a giving-natured meaning

toyada.why_not: Starts with English 'toy' and the full form reads feminine

navaja.name: Navaj
navaja.say_note: Simple consonants; final -a dropped in the Marathi/Hindi manner so Americans say nuh-VAHJ.
navaja.collisions: Close in sound to the common Navya/Nav- family but not itself in use
navaja.note: Clean two-syllable word meaning 'newborn, new' — apt for a first child and unused as a name.

pavana.why_not: Pavan is a very common name for Indian men of the parents' generation.

plaksha.name: Plaksha
plaksha.say_note: 'PLAK-shuh' is readable from the spelling; the ksh cluster is the only mild hurdle but Americans handle it as in 'Moksha'.
plaksha.note: A named sacred tree of Vedic geography; unusual, masculine and concrete.

bakula.why_not: Bakula is used as a girl's name in India and sounds feminine.

mahina.why_not: Reads feminine, and 'mahina' means 'month' in Hindi/Marathi everyday speech.

manada.why_not: Essentially a vocative epithet; sounds feminine and flat in English.
manada.collisions: Manada is a girl's name in Bengali usage

viruda.why_not: Reads like 'virus'/'viruda' oddly in English and the meaning (a panegyric poem) is not personal.

shaukla.why_not: Awkward cluster, reads like the surname Shukla.

samvaha.name: Samvah
samvaha.meaning: the wind that bears things along; one of the seven celestial winds
samvaha.say_note: sum-VAH; no aspirates in American reading, the h is simply silent at the end.
samvaha.note: Gives a natural American nickname 'Sam' while being a genuine Puranic wind-name.

samgita.why_not: Sangeeta is a well-known woman's name.

sujata.why_not: Sujata is an extremely common older woman's name.

sudaya.name: Sudaya
sudaya.say_note: Open vowels only; an American reads it correctly on sight.
sudaya.collisions: Faint echo of Sudhir/Udaya but distinct
sudaya.note: 'A good gift' — warm meaning, very easy to say, and essentially unused.

sumana.why_not: Reads as a feminine name (Sumana/Sumanā, also a flower).

sushumna.why_not: Consonant cluster is unpronounceable for Americans and the word is a yogic anatomical term.

acharya.why_not: A title and a common surname, not a given name.

rigveda.why_not: The name of a scripture; not usable as a personal name.

kalyanin.why_not: Grammatical -in stem; awkward ending and close to the feminine Kalyani.

kuta.why_not: Too short and invites bad English playground readings.

kshitipa.why_not: Kshi- cluster plus four syllables; Americans will mangle it.

kshetra.why_not: Means 'field/plot of land'; impersonal and hard to pronounce.

gotresha.why_not: Clunky, and 'gotra' reads as a clan-term rather than a name.

chandana.why_not: Chandan is a common older-generation name and Chandana reads feminine.

dyumani.name: Dyumani
dyumani.say_note: Americans read 'Dyu-' like the start of 'dew'; workable, though the initial cluster takes one correction.
dyumani.note: Beautiful poetic epithet of the sun, completely unused as a modern name.

natra.name: Natra
natra.meaning: a kind of dance (in the classical music treatises)
natra.say_note: Two clean syllables; no American will stumble.
natra.collisions: None; faintly echoes Natraj without being it
natra.note: Crisp, modern-sounding, and tied to the Nata/dance family of words.

naviyas.why_not: A comparative grammatical form; the -yas ending is awkward in English.

nishanka.name: Nishank
nishanka.say_note: nih-SHAHNK — spelled transparently, no aspirates or retroflexes for an English reader.
nishanka.collisions: Rare in India, essentially unused among Indian-Americans
nishanka.note: Strong virtue meaning (fearless) with an easy 'Nish' nickname.

nirmatri.why_not: An agent-noun stem; the -tri ending is clumsy and reads feminine in English.

nishnata.why_not: Retroflex-dependent and clunky; sounds like a mispronunciation of Nishant.

nripati.why_not: Initial 'Nri' is unpronounceable from the spelling for Americans.

nrivara.why_not: Same 'Nri' problem; also four-ish syllables and unfamiliar.

paktra.why_not: Harsh cluster and a technical ritual meaning; not name-like.

pitri.why_not: Means 'father/ancestor spirits'; cannot be given to a child.

pragatri.why_not: Agent-noun form with an awkward -tri ending.

pranayya.why_not: The -ayya ending reads South Indian and is mangled in English; too close to Pranay.

pradipa.why_not: Pradeep is a very common name for Indian men born 1950–1990.

manjula.why_not: Manjula is a well-established woman's name.

matamga.name: Matanga
matamga.meaning: elephant; by extension the finest of its kind
matamga.say_note: muh-TAHN-guh reads naturally; no aspirates or retroflex traps.
matamga.collisions: Known as a sage's name in the epics; not in modern baby use
matamga.note: Rare but genuine; strong imagery and an easy American short form 'Matt'.

ruchita.why_not: Ruchita is a girl's name in India.

lasya.why_not: Lasya is the graceful feminine dance and a girl's name.

variyas.why_not: Comparative grammatical form; awkward -yas ending for Americans

vasanta.name: Vasant
vasanta.say_note: Easy, but common among older Marathi men
vasanta.note: Real and lovely, but fails the older-generation test; included as usable only if parents accept a classic.

vadisha.why_not: Reads feminine in the USA due to -isha ending

vijnanin.why_not: jn cluster unpronounceable for Americans; grammatical possessive form

vivasvat.why_not: Final -vat cluster is clunky; Americans stumble; sounds like an epithet not a name

virahan.why_not: Deeply negative meaning (destroyer of sacred fire)

satkara.why_not: tk cluster reads oddly; abstract noun, not name-like

svarmani.why_not: Sv- cluster plus -mani reads feminine to Americans

hulla.why_not: Sounds comical in English (hullabaloo); ends -a feminine

aktu.why_not: Reads like an abbreviation; harsh kt cluster

arkin.name: Arkin
arkin.say_note: Spelled phonetically; Americans read it right first time
arkin.collisions: Similar to surname Arkin (Alan Arkin); no Indian-American popularity

archi.name: Archi
archi.say_note: Might be read as short for Archibald/Archie
archi.note: Easy and warm; Archie nickname may be a plus or a minus.

arhya.why_not: rhy cluster mangled by Americans; close to Arya

ishupa.why_not: Name of an Asura; negative association

rishu.why_not: Meaning uncertain in the dictionary; also a common Hindi pet name

kada.why_not: Reads oddly/feminine; 'kada' means bitter/sour in some Indian usages

kimba.why_not: Sounds like Kimba the lion cartoon / Kim; weak meaning

kritnu.why_not: tn cluster hard to say; unfamiliar shape

keta.why_not: Too close to Ketu/Keta girls' names; reads feminine in English

ketu.why_not: Ketu is the inauspicious shadow planet in Indian astrology

giri.name: Giri
giri.collisions: Common as element (Girish) and as a South Indian surname/name
giri.note: Solid meaning but slightly dated and g-sound ambiguity.

gritsa.why_not: Sounds like 'grits'; awkward in the USA

chaitra.name: Chaitra
chaitra.meaning: The spring month Chaitra, first month of the Hindu year
chaitra.say_note: Easy consonants; final -tra may get flattened
chaitra.collisions: Used as a girl's name in Karnataka; check family comfort
chaitra.note: Masculine in Sanskrit, but gender perception varies.

turni.why_not: Reads as 'turny'; feminine -i ending with weak appeal

tena.why_not: Reads as the girls' name Tena/Tina

tripura.why_not: Indian state name; also a goddess epithet (Tripura Sundari)

didi.why_not: 'Didi' means elder sister in Hindi/Marathi — strongly feminine

dipra.name: Dipra
dipra.say_note: No aspirates or retroflexes; reads cleanly
dipra.collisions: Rare; loosely echoes Deepak/Dipra Bengali usage
dipra.note: Fresh light-name, distinct from the very common Deep- names.

deshya.why_not: Means 'of the country/standard'; reads like 'desi', awkward

dyotin.name: Dyotin
dyotin.say_note: Dy- onset takes one beat to learn but is readable

druta.why_not: Also a tempo term; reads close to 'brute/drooty'; weak as a name

druma.name: Druma
druma.meaning: Tree; a tree of Indra's paradise
druma.collisions: Name of a Kimpurusha king in the Mahabharata; very rare today
druma.note: Nature meaning with a strong short nickname Dru.

nitya.why_not: Nitya is overwhelmingly a girl's name in India

nishna.name: Nishna
nishna.meaning: skilful, clever, deeply versed in a craft
nishna.say_note: Spelled phonetically; the sh-n cluster is the only small hurdle but Americans handle it as in 'Krishna'.
nishna.collisions: No common name collisions; faintly echoes Nishant/Krishna
nishna.note: Rare vocabulary word with a clean, flattering meaning; nickname Nish is friendly.

niloda.name: Niloda
niloda.meaning: one of blue waters; a river or sea of dark-blue water
niloda.say_note: Every sound is transparent from the spelling; no aspirates or retroflex traps.
niloda.collisions: Related to the very common Nilesh/Neel but not itself used
niloda.note: Keeps the familiar Marathi 'nil' (blue) root while being essentially unused as a name.

nuda.why_not: Reads as 'nude' to Americans; also a dubious dictionary variant.

neri.why_not: Reads as an Italian surname and as a girl's name; 'a kind of dance' is weak for a boy.
neri.note: Ambiguous gender in the source too (m. or f.).

pancha.why_not: Reads as English 'paunch'/'puncha' and is transparently the word for 'five'.

padvan.why_not: Sounds like a compound object/vehicle name in English; meaning 'road' is flat for a person.
padvan.note: Also a bare grammatical stem in -van.

pota.why_not: Means 'young animal'; invites 'potty'/'Potter' teasing and is vulgar-adjacent in Spanish.

prani.why_not: In modern Hindi/Marathi 'prani' simply means 'animal/creature', which would read oddly.

balin.name: Balin
balin.say_note: Two open syllables, no aspirates; Americans read it correctly on sight.
balin.collisions: A dwarf in Tolkien; distinct from Bali/Balram
balin.note: Clean strength meaning, crisp with Gawande, and virtually unused among Indian-American boys.

bimba.why_not: Reads as 'bimbo'; also used as a feminine word in Sanskrit poetry.

brahmi.why_not: Aspirated 'brahm' cluster, feminine form, and the name of an herb/script.

marya.why_not: Indistinguishable from Maria/Marya, a girl's name in the USA.

maha.why_not: Functions as a prefix, not a name; also a popular Arabic girl's name.

mama.why_not: Means 'uncle' and reads as 'mama' in English.

mriga.why_not: The 'mri' cluster is mangled by Americans; means 'wild animal/deer'.

moda.name: Moda
moda.collisions: Means 'fashion' in Italian/Spanish; echoes the surname Modi
moda.note: Warm, simple meaning; 'Mo' is an effortless American nickname.

raka.name: Raka
raka.say_note: Two open syllables, no tricky consonants.
raka.collisions: Homophonous with 'raka' (full-moon night), which is feminine in usage

rana.why_not: Reads as the common surname/title Rana and as Hindi 'ran' (battle); also a girl's name in Arabic.

roka.name: Roka

roka.collisions: 'Roca' (rock) in Spanish; 'rok'/'rokad' in Hindi means cash/cease
roka.note: Vedic light word, crisp and globally easy; check the Hindi 'rok' association with family.

rocha.name: Rocha
rocha.note: Same root as Ruchir/Rochak but unused as a given name.

rohana.why_not: Too close to the very common Rohan, and reads as feminine with the -a.

vapus.why_not: Reads like 'vapors'; -us stem is awkward as a name.

vartman.why_not: Means 'wheel-rut/path'; sounds like a compound word and is heavy in English.

varsha.why_not: Varsha is a well-established girl's name in India.

varda.name: Varda

varda.collisions: Varda is a Hebrew girl's name ('rose') and a cyclone name
varda.note: Masculine in Sanskrit with lovely monsoon imagery; the Hebrew feminine use is the one caveat.

vijna.why_not: The 'jn' cluster is unpronounceable from English spelling.

vedi.name: Vedi

shikva.why_not: The 'kv' cluster is awkward and it looks like 'shikwa' (Urdu for complaint).

shipi.why_not: Reads as 'ship-ee'; sounds childish and feminine.

shevya.name: Shevya
shevya.meaning: dear, to be cherished as a friend
shevya.say_note: The -vya glide takes one beat of practice but is readable; no aspirates.
shevya.collisions: Faint resemblance to Shreya (feminine), so spelling matters
shevya.note: Warm Vedic adjective, completely unused; the Shreya echo is the only risk.

shochis.why_not: The -is/-chis ending reads oddly in English and looks like a plural.

sahat.why_not: A bare participial stem; the final -t sounds clipped and unnamelike.

suri.why_not: Reads as a girl's name in the USA (Suri Cruise).

sushas.why_not: Reads as 'Sue-shass'; clunky and looks like a misspelling of Suhas.
sushas.note: Rejected; also too close to the older-generation Suhas.

syuma.why_not: The 'sy' onset is unpronounceable for Americans.

svarga.why_not: Religiously loaded ('heaven') and the 'svar-g' cluster gets mangled.

homa.why_not: A ritual act, not a person-word; also a Persian girl's name and reads as 'homer/homo' risk.

hlada.why_not: The 'hl' onset does not exist in English.

agaja.why_not: An adjective used mainly of Parvati/feminine referents; reads as a girl's name.

agira.name: Agira

agira.collisions: Close to the girl's name Amira in sound, but distinct in spelling
agira.note: Rare Vedic word for the sun; warm, bright meaning with an easy open-vowel shape for American ears.

agnija.why_not: Adjective 'fire-born', reads feminine (-ija) and is used for goddess epithets

arkaja.name: Arkaja
arkaja.say_note: All simple syllables; no aspirates or retroflexes
arkaja.collisions: Arjun/Arya are common; Arkaja is distinct
arkaja.note: Solar meaning tied to the root arka (sun); very rarely used, so it stays unique.

alati.why_not: Obscure lexical word for a song; reads feminine and like 'a latte'

avagja.why_not: Unpronounceable cluster and a negative technical meaning

ashoka.why_not: Famous emperor's name and common older-generation name (Ashok)

amnaya.name: Amnaya
amnaya.say_note: m-n sequence splits naturally across syllables; no tricky sounds
amnaya.collisions: Slight echo of Amaya (girl's name) but clearly distinct
amnaya.note: A weighty word for inherited learning — meaningful for an immigrant family passing on culture.

ishayu.name: Ishayu
ishayu.say_note: Reads phonetically; 'ish' is familiar to English speakers
ishayu.collisions: Ishaan is common; Ishayu is clearly different
ishayu.note: Vedic adjective for youthful strength; rare and cleanly pronounceable.

ugresha.why_not: Means 'terrible lord'; starts 'ugh/ugly' in English ears

udgama.why_not: dg cluster is awkward for Americans; reads like a word not a name

ullasa.why_not: Ullas is an established older-generation Marathi/Indian men's name

ritapa.name: Ritapa
ritapa.meaning: guardian of cosmic truth and order
ritapa.say_note: Simple consonants; only risk is 'Rit' vs 'Reet' vowel
ritapa.collisions: Rita is a Western girl's name, but Ritapa is unmistakably masculine in full
ritapa.note: Built on rita, the Vedic idea of truth/cosmic order — strong, principled meaning.

ekayu.name: Ekayu
ekayu.meaning: possessing the chief vigour of life
ekayu.note: Vedic word joining 'one' and 'life-force'; distinctive and easy to say.

kanishka.why_not: Well-known historical king's name and already in use; also used for girls

kuruha.why_not: Just means 'a tree'; awkward sound, echoes 'Kurus'

kekaya.why_not: A tribe/place name, not a personal name; sing-song and odd in English

kshaita.why_not: Ksh- cluster is unpronounceable for Americans

galaka.why_not: Means a small fish; also suggests 'gala'

garugi.why_not: Obscure musical term; sounds like 'gargle'/'Gucci' mashup

girija.why_not: Strongly established as a feminine name (Parvati)

giriraj.why_not: Common older-generation North Indian men's name

gupila.name: Gupila
gupila.say_note: Spelling is transparent; hard g must be assumed
gupila.collisions: No common-name clash; faint echo of 'Gupta' surname
gupila.note: Rare Unadi word meaning protector/king — strong sense, essentially unused as a name.

chauksha.why_not: ksh cluster; means merely 'clean', and 'Chauksha' is a Marathi adjective (chokha), not a name

tapana.why_not: Tapan is a common older-generation Indian men's name

taruja.why_not: Adjective 'produced by a tree'; reads feminine

tarendra.name: Tarendra
tarendra.say_note: Familiar pattern for Americans who know 'Rajendra'; -dra is manageable
tarendra.collisions: Rhymes with older names in -endra, but Tarendra itself is very rare
tarendra.note: Celestial and regal without being an -endra name of the grandparents' generation.

dayita.why_not: -ita ending reads feminine; used as a girl's name

davapa.why_not: Means one who watches a forest fire — odd, unappealing image

dasharha.why_not: sh-h sequence will be mangled; it is a clan epithet rather than a given name

divisha.name: Divish

divisha.say_note: Two clean syllables; no aspirates or retroflexes. Americans read it right on first try.

divisha.note: Dropping the final -a (as in Girish, Ramesh) keeps it masculine and crisp for the USA.

didivi.why_not: Reduplicated Vedic adjective; sounds like baby-talk and reads feminine in English.

dikshita.why_not: A ritual/priestly title and a common surname, with a ksh cluster Americans mangle; also dated.

dinara.why_not: Means a gold coin (a loanword from Latin denarius); Dinara is also a well-known Central Asian girl's name.

dyuratna.why_not: The initial dy- cluster and four-sound pileup make it unpronounceable for Americans.

narapa.why_not: Flat compound 'man-protector'; sounds like a nonsense word and invites 'Nap'.

naviya.why_not: The -iya ending reads distinctly feminine in Indian-American usage (cf. Navya, Kavya).

nisaru.why_not: Obscure technical term for a musical measure; no name-like weight and sounds unfinished.

nitara.why_not: Nitara is already established as a girl's name; meaning 'deeply fixed in the earth' is also weak for a person.

padavi.why_not: In modern Marathi/Hindi padavi means 'degree, title', so it reads as a common noun; -vi ending also skews feminine.

payoda.name: Payoda
payoda.say_note: All open syllables, no aspirates; the only risk is an American reading the first syllable as English 'pay', which still lands close enough.
payoda.collisions: Essentially unused as a given name; no English word collision
payoda.note: A classical Kalidasa-era poetic word for the monsoon cloud — generous, lyrical, and genuinely unused.

pushkara.why_not: Pushkar is an established, somewhat older-generation name, and the 'push' opening invites teasing.

pratika.why_not: Pratik is a very common name for Marathi men born 1970-1995; fails the older-generation test.

pragrya.why_not: The -gry- cluster is unpronounceable for American speakers.

prertvan.why_not: Consonant-heavy and unsayable; not name-shaped in any register.

manika.why_not: Manik is a common older-generation name and Manika reads as a girl's name.

maderu.why_not: Primary gloss is 'very intoxicating' and it opens with 'mad' in English.

mishraka.why_not: Means 'mixed / impure' — a weak, faintly negative meaning, and echoes the surname Mishra.

minara.why_not: Means a sea-monster; also reads as 'minaret'/a feminine name.

mainaka.name: Mainaka

mainaka.note: A lovely story name — the mountain who offered rest to Hanuman mid-flight. Strong, masculine, unmistakably Indian, and essentially unclaimed.

lokapa.why_not: Bare compound 'world-guardian' that reads like a title, not a name; final -pa is anticlimactic.

vanada.name: Vanada

vanada.collisions: Not in use as a given name; no English word collision
vanada.note: Reads nicely with Gawande and gives the ready-made American short form 'Van'.

vanapa.why_not: 'Woodman/forest-guard' is an occupational term; the -napa shape sounds like 'nap'.

varivas.why_not: A neuter abstract noun ending in -as; sounds like a Latin word or a lab term, not a boy's name.

vavata.why_not: Reduplicated Vedic form; sounds comical in English and would be misread.

vriksha.why_not: Initial vr- plus ksh is exactly the cluster Americans cannot produce; also just the plain word for 'tree'.

vrishan.why_not: Hard vr- onset, an -an ending the parents want to avoid, and the word also denotes a bull/virility with crude connotations.

vrishni.why_not: Primarily a clan name (Krishna's Vrishni clan), and the vr- onset plus -ni ending mispronounces badly.

vedisha.name: Vedish
vedisha.meaning: lord of knowledge; master of the Vedas, an epithet of Brahma
vedisha.say_note: Patterns exactly like Girish or Ramesh; Americans handle the -ish ending easily.
vedisha.collisions: Vedant/Ved are common, but Vedish itself is very rare; the -a form Vedisha would read feminine
vedisha.note: Familiar Sanskrit shape with a meaning the family can explain in one sentence, yet almost no one else uses it.

sharmin.why_not: Sharmin is an established feminine name in Bengali/Muslim usage, and it echoes the surname Sharma.

shimsha.why_not: Obscure tree name; the sh-...-sh shape is a tongue-twister and also a South Indian river name.

shushma.why_not: Indistinguishable from Sushma, a very common woman's name.

shushmi.why_not: Reads feminine and sounds like a pet-name diminutive in Hindi/Marathi.

shrutayu.name: Shrutayu
shrutayu.meaning: one whose life is devoted to sacred learning; name of a king of the solar dynasty
shrutayu.say_note: 'Shr-' is familiar from Shrek/shrewd, and the rest is fully phonetic; slightly long but never mangled.
shrutayu.collisions: Shruti is a common girl's name, but Shrutayu is clearly male and essentially unused today
shrutayu.note: A genuine Ramayana/Mahabharata king's name — dignified, learned, and completely unclaimed among Indian-American kids.

samura.why_not: Means a kind of deer valued for its skin; Americans will hear 'samurai', and the -ura ending reads feminine.

sahuri.why_not: The -uri ending reads feminine and it collides with Sahuri/Sahari-type names; also a bare Vedic adjective.

simika.why_not: Obscure tree name and the -ika ending is firmly feminine in Indian naming.

subahu.name: Subahu
subahu.meaning: strong-armed; one of handsome, capable arms — an epic prince's name
subahu.say_note: Every syllable is open and unaspirated; the spelling gives Americans the right sounds directly.
subahu.collisions: An epic name but not in modern circulation; no clash with popular baby names
subahu.note: Classical and strong; note 'bahu' also means daughter-in-law in Hindi, which some relatives may tease about.

sumaya.why_not: Sumaya/Sumayya is a well-established Arabic girl's name; would be read as female.

stavarha.why_not: The st-...-rha shape is unpronounceable from English spelling and looks like a typo.

havana.why_not: Reads as Havana, Cuba (and the pop song); no one would hear an Indian name.

holaka.why_not: Means half-cooked pulse; trivial, faintly comic food word.

amshumat.why_not: The -mat stem form is grammatical; Americans would mangle 'Amshu-', and Amshuman is an older-generation name.

agramshu.why_not: gr+msh cluster is unpronounceable for Americans; technical optics term.

anga.why_not: Primary sense is 'limb/body part'; reads oddly in English and invites teasing.

angarin.why_not: Root sense is 'charcoal/scorched'; an adjective, and feminine in usage.

angir.name: Angir
angir.meaning: Name of the sage who received the sacred knowledge from Atharvan and passed it on — a link in the chain of wisdom
angir.say_note: Two clean syllables, hard g; 'AN-geer' is the natural American reading.
angir.collisions: Echoes the better-known Angiras/Angira but is itself unused today.
angir.note: Dignified Vedic sage name that stays short and easy on a US roll call with Gawande.

anchati.why_not: A verb form (3rd person 'he bends/honours'), not a name; also reads feminine.

adarsha.why_not: Indistinguishable from the very common name Adarsh; also the dictionary sense here is 'moonless day'.

apsumat.why_not: Grammatical stem form, harsh consonant run, and reads like 'apps'.

ahladin.why_not: Contains the aspirated hl cluster the family wants to avoid; Americans read 'ah-LAD-in' (Aladdin).

ilya.why_not: Reads as the Russian name Ilya, not Indian; obscure mythic tree with no positive resonance.

uddipta.name: Uddipta
uddipta.say_note: Spelling steers Americans to 'oo-DEEP-ta'; no aspirates or retroflex traps, though the double d needs one correction sometimes.
uddipta.collisions: Shares the familiar 'deep' element with Deepak/Dipta but is unused as a name.
uddipta.note: Strong light imagery with a friendly built-in nickname, and nothing like it in Indian-American classrooms.

upajman.why_not: Obscure Vedic word, clumsy -jman ending Americans cannot parse.

ulka.why_not: Ulka is used as a girl's name (meteor, feminine ulkā) and reads like 'ulcer' to English ears.

ushat.why_not: American reading produces an unfortunate two-word pun; guaranteed playground problem.

ushasya.why_not: Dawn-related adjective that sounds distinctly feminine (Usha).

urjasvin.name: Urjasvin
urjasvin.meaning: Full of vital energy; powerful, vigorous, mighty
urjasvin.say_note: Every sound exists in English; 'oor-JAS-vin' comes out right, and the -vin ending feels name-like.
urjasvin.collisions: Related to Urja/Ojas but distinct; essentially unused.
urjasvin.note: Vedic vigour word with a masculine -in ending; 'Vin' is a nice American-friendly short form.

richa.why_not: Richa is an established girl's name in India.

kadamba.name: Kadamba
kadamba.meaning: The kadamba tree, with fragrant orange blossoms; a favourite of poets and associated with the monsoon and with Krishna
kadamba.say_note: Simple open syllables, no aspirates or retroflex sounds; Americans read it correctly on sight.
kadamba.collisions: Known as a dynasty/tree name but not used as a boy's first name today.
kadamba.note: Warm, poetic nature word that pairs well with Gawande and is unlikely to be duplicated.

kayya.why_not: Obscure prince's name, reads like the girls' name Kaya/Kaia.

karmanya.name: Karmanya
karmanya.meaning: Skilful in work; capable, diligent, industrious
karmanya.say_note: Clear three syllables; the retroflex n flattens harmlessly to English n.
karmanya.collisions: Recognisably built on karma, so meaning is half-guessable, yet the name itself is unused.
karmanya.note: A Rigvedic virtue word praising capable hands; sounds masculine and modern.

kala.why_not: Too many senses (black, time) and reads as the girls' name Kayla/Kala.

kachima.why_not: Very obscure lexical word; -ima ending sounds feminine.

karshana.why_not: The common sense of karshana is 'dragging, emaciating'; negative overtone.

kimshuka.name: Kinshuk
kimshuka.meaning: The flame-of-the-forest tree (Butea frondosa), famed for its brilliant blossoms
kimshuka.say_note: Spelled Kinshuk it reads cleanly as 'KIN-shook'; no aspirates or retroflexes.
kimshuka.collisions: A handful of bearers in India but rare and not current among Indian-American babies.
kimshuka.note: Vivid poetic tree name, crisp and short next to Gawande.

kisa.why_not: Reads as 'kissa/kisser' in English; too slight.

kulirad.why_not: Means 'crab-eating young crab' — absurd and unpleasant.

kushri.why_not: Obscure teacher's name; -shri ending reads feminine and the cluster is awkward.

kuhakka.why_not: Sounds comical in English and kuhaka means 'trickster/cheat'.

krikin.why_not: Harsh, nonsense-sounding in English ('creakin'); no meaning beyond an obscure king.

konva.why_not: Unattractive sound, obscure mountain, reads like 'convo'.

kraturaj.why_not: Kr- cluster plus four consonant runs; refers to the horse sacrifice, not child-friendly.

kshitija.why_not: Ksh- is unpronounceable for Americans and Kshitija is a girl's name in India.

garga.why_not: American ears hear 'gargle/gargoyle'; also a common Indian surname.

garhya.why_not: Aspirated rh cluster, and garhya separately means 'blameworthy'.

gatuvid.why_not: Compound adjective, not a name; ends in a clunky -vid that reads like 'video/vid'.

gida.why_not: Too slight and obscure; reads like 'Gita' misspelled and thus feminine.

girindra.name: Girindra
girindra.meaning: Lord of mountains; a great peak (also an epithet of Shiva)
girindra.say_note: Hard g and the familiar '-indra' pattern make 'gih-RIN-druh' the natural American reading.
girindra.collisions: Occasionally seen in Bengal historically; not in use among Indian-American babies.
girindra.note: Solid, masculine mountain name with Shiva resonance and a clean nickname in Giri.

geyajna.why_not: The -jna cluster is unpronounceable for Americans and the word is a descriptive adjective, not a name.

gopitri.why_not: Reads as a feminine -tri ending and is a grammatical agent noun; Americans would say 'go-pit-ree'.

gramagni.why_not: Means 'village fire' — a ritual object, not a personal name; also clumsy to say.

chanas.name: Chanas
chanas.say_note: Spelled phonetically for English; 'ch' as in chair, final -as like 'us'.
chanas.collisions: Faintly similar to Chandan/Chance but distinct.
chanas.note: A clean Vedic word for joy that works as a crisp two-syllable modern name.

champaka.why_not: Champak is an established older-generation Indian male name and invites 'Champ/Chomp' teasing.

jamatri.why_not: Means 'son-in-law' — an awkward kinship term, not a name.

jnana.why_not: The jñ- cluster is unpronounceable from the spelling for Americans; also an abstract neuter noun.

jnanagni.why_not: Four syllables with an impossible jñ- onset; philosophical term, not a name.

tamsu.name: Tamsu
tamsu.meaning: Name of a prince of the lunar dynasty in the Mahabharata
tamsu.say_note: Fully phonetic; no clusters or retroflexes.
tamsu.note: An obscure epic prince's name with a clean, modern two-syllable sound.

tattva.why_not: Abstract neuter philosophical noun; the -ttv- cluster is hard and it reads as jargon, not a name.

tallaja.why_not: Only used as a suffix meaning 'excellent specimen of'; also reads as 'tall' in English.

tunyu.why_not: Obscure tree name with a babyish, nickname-like sound.

turanya.name: Turanya
turanya.meaning: Swift; the name of one of the Moon's horses
turanya.say_note: Reads cleanly; slight risk of a feminine impression from -ya.
turanya.collisions: Not close to any common name.
turanya.note: Vivid image of a swift celestial horse; parents should be comfortable with the -ya ending.

taila.why_not: The ordinary Sanskrit word for 'oil'; unappealing meaning.

toyaraj.why_not: Begins with the English word 'toy'; guaranteed teasing.

tranga.why_not: Just a place-name of unclear reference, and listed as feminine too; no personal meaning.

tvaksara.why_not: Means 'having sound skin' — a medical adjective, unsuitable and hard to say.

tvarita.why_not: Tv- onset defeats English speakers, and the -ita form reads feminine (Tvarita is a goddess epithet).

dala.why_not: Bare word for 'leaf/piece'; too slight and reads like a filler syllable in English.

davagni.why_not: Means 'forest fire' — a destructive image, not auspicious for a child.

diti.why_not: Overwhelmingly known as the female mother of the demons; reads feminine.

dikkarin.why_not: The first syllable is an obscene English word; unusable.

dikpati.why_not: Same obscene-sounding first syllable in American English.

dishana.name: Dishan
dishana.meaning: An instructor in sacred knowledge; one who shows the way
dishana.say_note: Shortened to Dishan so Americans read it right; no tricky sounds.
dishana.collisions: Near Dhruvan/Rishaan but clearly its own name.
dishana.note: Strong 'guide/teacher' meaning with an easy, contemporary sound.

diptimat.why_not: The -mat suffix reads as the English word 'mat' and the whole is a grammatical possessive form.

duda.why_not: Reads as 'dude/doo-doo' in American English; obscure mountain name.

duru.why_not: Obscure mountain name with a weak, nickname-like sound.

duli.why_not: Sounds feminine/diminutive in English and Marathi ears alike.

durva.why_not: Durva is chiefly known as the sacred grass and is used as a girl's name in Maharashtra.

devarha.why_not: Adjective 'worthy of the gods' with an awkward -rha cluster no American will say.

dyupati.why_not: Dy- onset is unreadable for Americans ('dye-you-patty').

dyumni.why_not: Dy- plus -mni cluster; Americans cannot get it from the spelling.

dyokara.why_not: A commentator's gloss, not a name; dy- onset also fails the pronunciation test.

dyutana.why_not: Lovely meaning but 'Dy-' is mispronounced by English speakers as 'die-'.

nakraraj.why_not: Means 'king of crocodiles/sharks'; unattractive and clumsy.

nagaukas.why_not: The -aukas ending is unreadable in English and the word is a lexicon gloss for 'lion'.

nandaka.name: Nandaka
nandaka.meaning: Joy, delight; also the name of Vishnu's sword
nandaka.say_note: All open syllables, no clusters; stress on the first.
nandaka.collisions: Related to the common Nandan/Nandkumar but itself rare for babies.
nandaka.note: Joyful meaning plus the heroic sword association; fresh while sounding familiar.

nandanta.name: Nandanta
nandanta.say_note: Phonetic and rhythmic for English speakers.
nandanta.note: A warm 'joyful son' meaning in an unusual form nobody else is using.

nandi.why_not: Instantly read as Shiva's bull, and Nandi is also a common African girl's name in the US.

naresha.why_not: Naresh is a very common name for Indian men born 1950–1985.

nardita.why_not: Means a dice throw; also sounds feminine.

nirjara.name: Nirjara
nirjara.collisions: Close to Nirjala (a fast day); minor

nirvata.why_not: Means windless/still; reads as odd and close to nirvat/nirvana confusion.

nisvana.name: Nisvan
nisvana.say_note: Short and phonetic; 'vn' blend is easy.
nisvana.note: Rare sound-themed name; Nisvan trims the final -a.

nripala.why_not: 'Nrip-' cluster hard for Americans; also older-generation flavor.

panchama.name: Pancham
panchama.meaning: the fifth note of the musical scale
panchama.collisions: R.D. Burman's nickname 'Pancham' — a fond association
panchama.note: Strong music meaning; rare as a given name today.

patman.why_not: Reads as English 'Pat man'; bad nickname risk.

padmadi.why_not: Grammatical compound 'lotus etc.'; not a name.

padmaka.why_not: Means lotus-shaped army formation; the -ka ending sounds diminutive.

panipnat.why_not: Intensive participle form, unpronounceable and odd.

parvata.why_not: Means mountain but reads as the common word/Parvati association, feminine pull.

pavitrin.why_not: Adjectival -in stem; too close to common Pavitra and sounds feminine.

pankta.why_not: A kind of Soma; reads awkwardly, near English 'punked'.

purishya.why_not: Root puriṣa also means excrement; unacceptable.

pushpa.why_not: Strongly a girl's name in India.

putadru.why_not: Reads as 'poo-'; bad start and obscure meaning.

putrima.why_not: Reads as 'poo-'; also close to putri (daughter).

paija.why_not: Obscure, meaningless to family, odd sound.

pragama.why_not: Means first advance in courtship; inappropriate.

prajapa.why_not: Awkward; evokes Prajapati and 'japa'; weak as a name.

pranada.why_not: Means yell/roar; also reads near 'Prana-da' confusion.

pranayin.why_not: Sounds feminine (Pranayi/Pranaya) and is an -in adjective stem.

pranetri.name: Pranet
pranetri.say_note: Pranet is easy; the -tri stem form would be mangled.
pranetri.collisions: Near Praneet/Praneeth, which are more common — slight overlap

pradavya.why_not: Means forest fire; destructive and clunky.

prabarha.why_not: Awkward 'rh' cluster; Americans would mangle it.

pramada.why_not: Identical in sound to pramadā (woman) and 'pramad' also means negligence; risky.

pramoda.name: Pramod
pramoda.say_note: Easy read, but American 'PRAY-mod' risk is low.
pramoda.collisions: Common for Indian men born 1950–1985 — a real drawback
pramoda.note: Usable and meaningful, but dates to the parents' parents' generation.

pravala.name: Praval
pravala.meaning: new shoot, young sprout; also coral
pravala.say_note: Spelling maps cleanly; no tricky sounds.
pravala.note: Lovely 'new growth' image, fitting for a firstborn.

prasadin.why_not: -in adjective stem; too close to older-generation Prasad.

prastava.why_not: Reads as a technical liturgical term and Americans see 'prostate/pasta' mangling; awkward.

prahlada.why_not: Very well-known older-generation Puranic name; also aspirated 'hl' cluster.

pravitri.why_not: Ends in -i/-tri, reads feminine and is a grammatical agent form.

bappa.why_not: In Marathi 'bappa' means father/Ganpati Bappa — reads as a nickname, not a given name.

baliyas.why_not: Comparative grammatical form; ends in -yas, odd in English.

balendu.name: Balendu
balendu.collisions: Rare as a given name today
balendu.note: Poetic Kalidasa-era word, fresh as a name.

brahmana.why_not: Caste term, not a personal name; aspirated cluster.

manchaka.why_not: Also means 'cot/bed'; sounds comic in English.

mati.why_not: Reads feminine and clashes with common word 'mati' (mind) and Italian names.

manasvin.name: Manasvin
manasvin.meaning: full of mind; intelligent, wise, spirited
manasvin.say_note: Spelled as read; -vin ending is easy.
manasvin.collisions: Manas is common; Manasvin is rare
manasvin.note: Handsome nickname Vin works in the US.

manishin.why_not: Too close to the very common older name Manish.

mahatman.why_not: Inseparable from Mahatma Gandhi; presumptuous as a name.

masanta.why_not: Means 'end of month' — weak, calendrical meaning.

munindra.why_not: Established older-generation name (esp. Bengali/Buddhist); not fresh.

maunda.why_not: Close to 'munda' (shaven head); obscure teacher name, no good meaning.

yaksha.why_not: Class of spirits, sometimes ominous; also 'Yakshi' feminine association.

yaju.name: Yaju
yaju.meaning: name of one of the ten horses of the Moon; linked to sacred Yajus verse

yajnaraj.why_not: 'jn' cluster is mangled by Americans; heavy ritual compound.

yashovat.name: Yashovat
yashovat.collisions: Yash is common, Yashovat is not
yashovat.note: Gives the familiar nickname Yash without the popularity.

yaunika.why_not: Root yoni association makes it unusable.

ratnaraj.name: Ratnaraj
ratnaraj.say_note: Both halves are familiar to American ears (Raj).

ramra.why_not: Consonant cluster 'mr' is hard; too close to Ram/Rama.

rajaraj.why_not: Repetitive; strongly associated with Chola/South-Indian Rajaraja.

rajin.name: Rajin
rajin.meaning: shining, royal one; a horse of the Moon
rajin.collisions: Close to Rajan but distinct and much rarer

rissu.why_not: Obscure poet's name with no meaning; sounds odd in English.

rupasvin.name: Rupasvin
rupasvin.note: Masculine -vin ending keeps it from sounding feminine.

reknas.why_not: Ends in harsh -nas, looks like 'wreck'; neuter noun.

raiva.why_not: Reads as a girl's name (Raiva/Reva) and Reva is a river goddess name.

rochas.why_not: Reads as Spanish surname Rochas/'roaches'; neuter noun.

rohanta.name: Rohanta
rohanta.meaning: a growing tree; that which rises and grows
rohanta.collisions: Rohan is common; Rohanta is distinct
rohanta.note: Pleasant growth imagery, though close to Rohan.

rohisha.why_not: A kind of grass; slight feminine -isha reading.

rauhina.why_not: Also the name of a demon slain by Indra; ambiguous and feminine-looking.

lokakrit.why_not: Three-plus syllables with awkward -krit cluster; reads as grammatical compound, hard to say.

varutri.why_not: Ends in -tri, reads feminine and is an agent-noun form.

varin.name: Varin
varin.meaning: Rich in gifts; name of a divine being among the Vishve Devah
varin.note: Clean, short, easy; slight echo of common Varun is the only risk.

variman.name: Variman
variman.note: Reads well in the USA, unused as a baby name.

varcha.why_not: Too close to varcha/varchas 'luster' but as given is an obscure sage; 'ch' ending sounds truncated and odd.

varnaka.why_not: Means a strolling player; weak meaning and ends -aka, sounds diminutive.

varnu.why_not: Just a river/district name; no personal-name value and sounds unfinished.

valguka.why_not: 'Valg-' cluster is unattractive in English; -uka sounds comic.

vatashva.why_not: Four syllables with -shv- cluster Americans cannot say.

vaganta.why_not: Means 'end of voice'; reads as 'vagant', awkward and near an unfortunate English root.

vagguli.why_not: Means betel-bearer, a servant role; sounds silly in English.

vadiraj.why_not: Established South-Indian (Madhva) saint's name; also 4 syllables.

vahitri.why_not: -tri agent form reads feminine in English.

vitamas.why_not: Americans read it as 'vitamins/vitamin'; instant teasing.

vipadma.why_not: Means 'deprived of a lotus' — negative meaning.

vikasat.why_not: Participial form, and looks like the brand/word 'Vikas' plus a suffix.

vikashin.name: Vikashin
vikashin.say_note: Spelled phonetically; 'sh' is safe for Americans.
vikashin.collisions: Echoes common older name Vikas, but distinct form
vikashin.note: Great nickname Kash; clear positive meaning.

vinka.why_not: Reads like 'Vinca'/'Vinnie'; obscure poet's name with no meaning.

vijanat.why_not: Present participle, not a name; ends flatly in -at.

vittada.why_not: Ends in -a and reads feminine; 'wealth-giver' sounds transactional.

vittesha.why_not: Epithet of Kubera, wealth-lord; ends -esha, sounds heavy and dated.

vidipta.name: Vidipta
vidipta.collisions: Related to common Deep/Dipta but itself unused

vinta.why_not: Obscure being with no meaning; reads like 'Vinta' vintage/female name.

virokin.name: Virokin
virokin.say_note: Every sound exists in English; stress falls naturally on ROH.

vilasin.why_not: In modern Indian usage vilasi connotes pleasure-seeking/indulgent; also used as a feminine name Vilasini.

vishpati.why_not: Four syllables; 'Vish' reads as poison to Indian ears and 'pati' as husband.

visa.why_not: Reads exactly as the English word 'visa' / credit card.

vyomin.name: Vyomin
vyomin.meaning: Of the sky; one belonging to the heavens (a celestial horse of the Moon)
vyomin.say_note: Initial vy- takes a beat but Americans manage 'vee-OH-min' acceptably.
vyomin.collisions: Vyom exists but is uncommon in the USA
vyomin.note: Lovely sky imagery; nickname Om is meaningful.

shakvara.name: Shakvara
shakvara.say_note: 'kv' is a mild hurdle but readable; no aspirates.

shavaka.why_not: Means 'the young of an animal'; also echoes shava (corpse).

shukra.why_not: Shukra is Venus/the asura-guru and also means semen; not usable.

shuna.why_not: Homophonous with shuna 'dog'; also reads feminine.

shritala.why_not: A palm-like tree; sounds feminine and like 'Sheetal'.

shvasana.why_not: Means breathing/wind but reads as 'shvas' (breath/sigh); initial shv- is hard and it is four syllables.

shahji.why_not: Name of a specific historical king and reads as an honorific with -ji; not a usable given name

samchara.why_not: Means 'passage/road'; weak, impersonal meaning and clunky in English

samja.name: Samaj
samja.meaning: the universal creator; an epithet of Brahma/Shiva
samja.say_note: Two clean syllables; no aspirates or retroflexes
samja.collisions: Close in sound to the Hindi word samaj ('society'), which parents should weigh
samja.note: Gives the ready-made American nickname Sam while staying fully Sanskrit.

satkavi.name: Satkavi
satkavi.say_note: All open syllables; Americans read it phonetically

sadvidya.why_not: Vidya reads strongly feminine in Indian-American usage

samtani.why_not: Santani is a known Sindhi surname and the -ani ending reads as a family name, not a boy's first name

samtapa.why_not: Means burning heat and, in usage, torment or grief — negative

samuhya.why_not: A technical ritual term (a kind of sacrificial fire) and a grammatical gerundive form

sammada.name: Sammad
sammada.say_note: Simple consonants; final -a dropped as is normal in North-Indian usage
sammada.note: A warm, positive meaning and an easy American-friendly shape.

samicha.why_not: Reads feminine in English (like Samantha/Michaela blends) despite masculine gender

samraj.name: Samraj
samraj.meaning: supreme or universal ruler (a Vedic epithet of Varuna and Indra)
samraj.say_note: Two strong syllables, entirely phonetic for Americans
samraj.collisions: Related to the common word samrat; Samraj also occurs as a surname in the south
samraj.note: Very sturdy, gives both Sam and Raj as nicknames.

sahasya.name: Sahasya
sahasya.say_note: No aspirates or retroflexes; the -sya ending is easy
sahasya.collisions: Near the common word sahas and the rarer name Sahasra
sahasya.note: Rigvedic word for strength, virtually unused as a modern name.

sakasha.why_not: Adjectival technical term; the sh-cluster spelling invites mangling and it sounds close to Aakash

sagnika.why_not: The -ika ending reads feminine and the first syllable reads as English 'sag'

sananda.why_not: Sananda is widely used as a girl's name and also an older-generation Ananda variant

saravat.why_not: Reads like a place or brand name in English and the -vat suffix is a bare grammatical ending

sukratu.name: Sukratu
sukratu.meaning: skilful and wise; of good purpose (said of the gods in the Rigveda)
sukratu.say_note: Clean kr cluster, no aspirates; spelled exactly as read
sukratu.collisions: Echoes Kratu, a Vedic sage name
sukratu.note: A genuinely rare Rigvedic epithet with an excellent meaning.

sukvana.why_not: The kv cluster is awkward for American speakers and the word is obscure lexicon-only

sukti.why_not: Two-consonant-cluster word meaning 'aphorism/oyster-shell'; reads feminine and is a common noun

sugriva.why_not: Strongly identified with the monkey king of the Ramayana; invites teasing

sucharu.name: Sucharu
sucharu.say_note: Phonetic, though the 'ch' must be read as in 'chair'
sucharu.collisions: Charu alone is mostly feminine in modern India; Sucharu is masculine in the epics
sucharu.note: Masculine in Mahabharata usage; parents should be comfortable with the softer feel.

sujavas.why_not: Ends in a Vedic -as stem that looks like a typo in English; awkward

sujihva.why_not: Means 'good-tongued'; the jihva cluster is unpronounceable for Americans

sujyotis.why_not: Jyoti reads feminine and the -tis ending is an awkward Vedic stem

sudipta.why_not: A very common name for Indian men born 1950–1995, especially Bengali

supeshas.why_not: Vedic -as stem; awkward spelling and unclear pronunciation in English

suranga.name: Suranga
suranga.meaning: beautiful colour; bright-hued (also the orange tree)
suranga.say_note: Fully phonetic, though the middle syllable reads as English 'rung'
suranga.collisions: In Hindi/Marathi surang can also mean a tunnel or mine
suranga.note: Pretty colour meaning, but the 'tunnel' sense in Marathi is worth considering.

sura.why_not: Also the common word for liquor/wine; too ambiguous

surunga.why_not: Obscure lexicon word for the drumstick tree; no name value

susheva.why_not: Reads feminine in English and the sh-v sequence is hard to say

susvamin.why_not: A descriptive compound ('a good master'), not name-like; sv cluster is difficult

suhastya.why_not: Means 'skilful-handed' but reads oddly and contains 'hasty' in English

suhasin.why_not: Too close to Suhas, a very common name for Maharashtrian men born 1950–1995

suktika.why_not: The -ika ending reads clearly feminine; also just an instrument name

srimara.why_not: Names an animal and contains 'mara' (death/killing) — negative

saumana.name: Sauman
saumana.say_note: Two syllables, all easy sounds; 'au' read as in 'sauna'
saumana.collisions: Resembles Sauman/Soman, a surname in some regions
saumana.note: Also carries the sumanas sense of 'good-hearted', which strengthens it.

sauri.why_not: Denotes Saturn (inauspicious connotation) and reads as a girl's name in English

stotra.why_not: A ritual genre term, not a personal name; the st- cluster plus -tra is unwieldy

stotriya.why_not: Purely a technical liturgical adjective; unusable as a name

spandana.why_not: Spandana is established as a girl's name in India

srotas.why_not: Ends in -as and opens with a hard 'sr-' cluster; Americans read it as 'scrotum'-adjacent. Unusable.

svarnaka.why_not: 'Sv-' cluster is mangled by English speakers, and it just means a kind of tree; too close to Swarna, read as feminine.

hinkara.why_not: Means a ritual grunting sound; weak, odd meaning and invites 'Hinky' nicknames.

hila.why_not: Two light syllables reading as a feminine name; also only a place name with no real meaning.

hushka.why_not: Reads as 'husk'/'hush'; harsh cluster and no usable meaning.

akopa.name: Akopa
akopa.meaning: free from anger; even-tempered — also the name of a wise minister of King Dasharatha
akopa.say_note: All open syllables, no clusters; the long O carries it.
akopa.collisions: No common name collisions; faintly echoes Akop (Armenian Hakob) which is harmless.
akopa.note: A genuine Ramayana minister's name with a clean virtue meaning — calm, anger-free. Very rare today.

akshu.why_not: 'kshu' is hard for Americans and the meaning ('a kind of net') is weak.

agasti.name: Agasti
agasti.meaning: the sage Agasti, the rishi who drank the ocean; 'mover of mountains'
agasti.say_note: Clean consonants; Americans may hear an echo of 'Augustus', which helps rather than hurts.
agasti.collisions: Close to the better-known Agastya; also near English Augustine/Augusto.
agasti.note: Real rishi name, rarely used in this shorter form. The 'Gus' nickname is a genuine bonus in the USA.

atisha.why_not: Widely read as feminine (Atishi) and it is really the title of a known Buddhist teacher, not a free name.

atka.why_not: Harsh, clipped and meaningless-sounding to an American ear; 'traveller' is a lexicon gloss only.

atna.name: Atna
atna.say_note: Two syllables, no clusters English can't handle; the t is a plain t.
atna.collisions: Slight echo of Etna (the volcano) — distinct enough in speech.
atna.note: Rare lexical word for the sun, from the root meaning 'to move constantly'. Truly unused as a name.

atya.why_not: Really an adjective form; the -tya ending reads feminine and gets mispronounced 'at-ee-ya'.

abjaja.why_not: The 'bj' cluster plus repeated -ja is clumsy in English; sounds like a stammer.

amaru.name: Amaru
amaru.meaning: the poet-king Amaru, author of the Amaru-shataka; from amara, 'undying'
amaru.say_note: Fully phonetic, open vowels, no cluster at all.
amaru.collisions: Also an Andean word (Tupac Amaru) — a known but non-conflicting association.
amaru.note: A real classical poet-king's name, connected to amara 'immortal'. Sounds fresh and is effortless for Americans.

ambaka.why_not: Amba is a goddess/feminine element; the name reads female and slightly comic in English.

ariha.name: Ariha
ariha.meaning: conqueror of foes; name of an ancient prince of the lunar line
ariha.say_note: Simple open syllables; the h is lightly voiced and forgiving.
ariha.collisions: Near the girls' name Ariha/Arihaa in some lists, but the Mahabharata prince is male.
ariha.note: 'Ari' is an easy, well-liked short form in the USA while the full name stays Indian and rare.

archat.why_not: A present participle, not a name, and the -at ending sounds unfinished in English.

archin.name: Archin
archin.meaning: shining, radiant; possessing rays of light
archin.say_note: Reads exactly as spelled for an American; stress naturally lands on the first syllable.
archin.collisions: Adjacent to Archit/Arjun but distinct; second syllable is the word 'chin', a mild but harmless overlap.
archin.note: Vedic word for radiance; gives the very American nickname Archie without being an English name.

arna.why_not: Reads as a feminine name in English (Arna/Arnaa) and sounds like a clipping of the very popular Arnav.

arvan.name: Arvan
arvan.meaning: swift, coursing; the swift one, said of Agni and Indra
arvan.say_note: Impossible to mispronounce; patterns like Arvin/Evan for American ears.
arvan.collisions: Close to Arvin and Arav/Arnav, but the spelling and meaning are its own.
arvan.note: Genuine Rigvedic adjective for swiftness; crisp, masculine, and essentially unused as a given name.

alas.why_not: Means 'not shining' (negative) and is the English interjection 'alas'.

avanti.why_not: Established as a girl's name in Marathi families (and the -i ending reads feminine).

avosha.why_not: 'King of ants' is a comic meaning; no defensible sense for a child.

akriti.why_not: Akriti/Aakriti is a well-established girl's name in India.

apva.why_not: Unpronounceable 'pv' cluster and a doubtful, disputed meaning.

ashu.why_not: Reads as a nickname (Ashu is the pet form of Ashutosh/Ashwin) rather than a full name.

asuri.why_not: Derived from asura (demon) and the -i ending reads feminine; bad associations.

ahuka.why_not: Americans hear 'a hookah'; unfortunate schoolyard sound.

induja.name: Induja
induja.meaning: son of the moon — the planet Mercury, planet of intellect
induja.say_note: Phonetic and smooth; only risk is a first-syllable stress, easily corrected.
induja.collisions: Indu alone is feminine in Hindi, but Induja is explicitly masculine ('son of').
induja.note: A real astronomical name for Mercury, the graha of intelligence and speech — lovely and unused.

ishya.why_not: Reads feminine (Ishya/Isha) and the -shya ending trips English speakers.

ukshan.why_not: 'ksh' is a mangler, and 'ox/bull' is a blunt meaning for a child.

utpala.why_not: Utpal is a common older-generation Indian man's name, and the -a form reads feminine.

utsa.name: Utsa
utsa.meaning: a spring, fountain, wellspring; the source from which waters rise
utsa.say_note: 'ts' mid-word is fine for English (like 'outset'); short and clean.
utsa.collisions: Shares a root with the common Utsav; used as a girl's name in Bengali, but is grammatically masculine.
utsa.note: A crisp Vedic word for a wellspring — strong 'source of good things' meaning for a first child.

udra.why_not: Means otter/crab; the 'dr' plus meaning gives no dignity, and it sounds like 'udder'.

upagu.why_not: Obscure king's name with no transparent meaning; 'goo' ending invites teasing.

umesha.why_not: Umesh is a very common name for Indian men born 1950–1990.

urasha.why_not: Bare sage name with no usable meaning; the -asha ending reads feminine in the USA.

ulanda.why_not: Sounds like Uganda/Yolanda; no meaning and reads feminine.

ushika.why_not: The -ika ending is distinctly feminine; obscure king's name with no meaning.

usha.why_not: Usha is a well-known woman's name in India, and of the older generation.

urvya.why_not: Obscure adjective about submarine fire; sounds feminine and unpronounceable cluster.

urja.name: Urja
urja.meaning: Strong, powerful, full of vigor and energy
urja.say_note: Two clean syllables, no aspirates; Americans read it correctly.
urja.collisions: Urja is sometimes used for girls as 'energy'; Urjit is the more common male form
urja.note: Rare and vigorous, though slightly unisex-leaning.

urjin.name: Urjin
urjin.collisions: Close to the known name Urjit
urjin.note: Clearly masculine and essentially unused in the US.

rikva.why_not: Initial vocalic r plus cluster; Americans mangle it and it looks harsh.

rigmin.why_not: Reads as 'rig-min', clunky and unattractive in English.

rijuka.why_not: Place name with -ka diminutive; three syllables ending in -a reads feminine and vague.

ekanga.why_not: 'Ekanga' also means one-limbed/paralysed in common usage — negative.

emusha.why_not: Name of a boar; ends -usha, reads feminine and odd.

eluka.why_not: Obscure substance; sounds too close to 'Uluka' (owl) and feminine.

evara.why_not: Etymology doubtful, no defensible meaning; reads like 'ever'.

kanka.why_not: Means heron but sounds comic in English; invites 'Conk'.

kanku.why_not: A millet seed; trivial meaning and silly sound.

kanta.why_not: Kanta is overwhelmingly a feminine/older-generation element in India.

kamya.why_not: Kamya is an established girls' name in India.

kartri.why_not: Grammatical agent noun; final -tri cluster is unpronounceable for Americans.

kavya.why_not: Kavya is a very popular girls' name.

kavyat.why_not: Grammatical participle form, not a usable name.

kavela.why_not: Lotus word but reads feminine and like 'Kayla/Cavella'.

kahva.why_not: Crane species; awkward 'hv' cluster and resembles 'kahwa' (coffee).

kagni.why_not: Means 'a little fire' — diminishing, and gn cluster is mispronounced.

kaneri.name: Kaneri
kaneri.meaning: Name of an ancient Sanskrit teacher
kaneri.say_note: All open syllables, no clusters; easy for Americans.
kaneri.collisions: Kanheri caves in Maharashtra — a pleasant local echo
kaneri.note: Unused as a modern name; teacher association is dignified.

karu.name: Karu
karu.meaning: Maker, artisan, craftsman; also a singer of praise
karu.say_note: Two simple syllables, impossible to mispronounce.
karu.collisions: Similar to Karan/Kabir but distinct; Karu is also a Tamil element, though the Sanskrit word is pan-Indian
karu.note: Short, warm, creative meaning; pairs well with Gawande.

kashin.name: Kashin
kashin.say_note: Spelling gives the sound directly; no aspirates.
kashin.collisions: Echoes Kashi (Varanasi) and the surname Cashin
kashin.note: Modern-sounding, very rare, strong light meaning.

kija.why_not: Obscure instrument word with uncertain sense; meaningless as a name.

kujapa.why_not: Ku- prefix reads as 'bad'; obscure astrological patronymic.

kunika.why_not: Reads feminine in English and in Indian usage (Kanika/Kunika).

kunin.why_not: Means a kind of savage — negative meaning.

kunda.name: Kunda
kunda.meaning: The white jasmine flower, an emblem of purity
kunda.say_note: Straightforward; slight risk of 'KUN-da' rhyme with Honda.
kunda.collisions: Kundan is a more familiar older name; flower names can lean feminine
kunda.note: Masculine in Sanskrit gender, but flower sense is soft.

kumba.why_not: A woman's head-dress; feminine and close to 'Kumbha'.

kuruka.why_not: Obscure prince variant; sounds like a bird call / 'kooky'.

kulin.name: Kulin
kulin.say_note: Phonetic and clean for American readers.
kulin.collisions: Used in Gujarat/Bengal, somewhat older-generation there
kulin.note: Rare among Indian-Americans today; dignified meaning.

kusuma.why_not: Strongly a girls' name in India.

kencha.why_not: A sparrow species; sounds like 'ketch-a' and is Kannada-flavored.

kenava.name: Kenava
kenava.meaning: Name of an ancient teacher, pupil of Shakapurni
kenava.note: Gives the ready American nickname Ken.

kendu.why_not: Ebony tree, obscure; reads like 'can do' / Kendall blend.

koli.why_not: Koli is a Maharashtrian caste/community name — unsuitable as a first name.

kosha.why_not: Means a cask/sheath; common vocabulary word (treasury) and reads feminine with the -a ending

koshin.why_not: Just a lexical word for the mango tree; no name feel and no real meaning for a person

kohin.why_not: Obscure plant word; reads like 'Cohen' in the USA

kauncha.why_not: Americans would mangle the au+ncha cluster; also a doubtful variant spelling

kaulya.name: Kaulya
kaulya.meaning: Born of a noble family; of good lineage
kaulya.say_note: Spelling maps cleanly: 'Kaul' as in 'cowl' plus -ya
kaulya.collisions: Kaul is a Kashmiri surname, but rare as a given name
kaulya.note: Dignified meaning about family lineage, fitting for a first-generation American child

knasa.why_not: Initial kn- cluster is unpronounceable for Americans and the meaning is uncertain

kramu.why_not: Means betel-nut tree; sounds like an odd fragment, no name quality

kroncha.why_not: Harsh consonant cluster, would be mispronounced; obscure mountain name

kledan.why_not: kl- cluster is awkward and the root sense (moistening) is unappealing

kledu.why_not: Awkward kl- onset; also echoes 'kled/klesha' (affliction) to Indian ears

kvayi.why_not: kv- onset is unpronounceable in English and the meaning is just 'some bird'

kshara.why_not: ksh- is hard for Americans and kshara also means caustic/alkali and 'perishable'

kshina.why_not: Means wasted, diminished, destroyed — clearly negative

kshupa.why_not: Means a small bush; weak meaning plus difficult ksh- onset

kshona.why_not: Difficult ksh- onset; also glossed as 'decay' in commentaries

ganga.why_not: Overwhelmingly read as the river Ganga, a feminine name

gani.name: Gani
gani.meaning: One versed in the scriptures and the sciences; a learned teacher (Jain honorific)
gani.say_note: Two open syllables, no clusters; reads exactly as spelled
gani.collisions: Ghani/Gani exists as a Muslim surname; still very rare as a boy's given name
gani.note: Scholarly Jain title; uncommon and easy for American teachers to say

gantu.name: Gantu
gantu.meaning: A way, a course; that which goes forward
gantu.note: Rigvedic word for 'path/course' — a clean, unused two-syllable option

gaya.why_not: Reads as 'gay-a' in English, inviting teasing; also a place name (Bodh Gaya)

gali.why_not: In Hindi/Marathi 'gali/gaali' means alley or abuse/swear word

galu.why_not: Obscure gem word; sounds like a nonsense syllable in English

gatri.name: Gatri
gatri.meaning: A singer; one who sings praise
gatri.say_note: Reads easily; the -tri ending is familiar from words like 'mantra'
gatri.collisions: Slight echo of Gayatri (feminine) — worth noting
gatri.note: Upanishadic agent noun for 'singer'; masculine in grammar but the Gayatri echo is a mild risk

gishnu.name: Gishnu
gishnu.meaning: A singer; one skilled in song
gishnu.collisions: Faintly echoes Vishnu/Jishnu but is distinct
gishnu.note: Rare musical word with a crisp, modern two-syllable shape

guhila.name: Guhila
guhila.meaning: Name of the prince who founded the Guhila (Sisodia) line of Mewar
guhila.say_note: All open syllables; Americans read it correctly
guhila.collisions: Known historically as a clan name, essentially unused as a given name today
guhila.note: Historic Rajput dynastic name — distinctive and honorable

geya.why_not: Grammatical participle ('to be sung'); reads as 'gay-a' in English

geshna.why_not: The -na/-a ending reads feminine in the USA, and Geshnu covers the same sense better

geshnu.name: Geshnu
geshnu.note: Vedic-era word for a performing musician; unique and easy

goja.why_not: Meaning ('produced by milk') is odd for a person and it reads awkwardly in English

gopa.why_not: Plain word for cowherd; too close to older-generation Gopal and the -a ending reads feminine (Gopa was Buddha's wife)

golava.name: Golava
golava.meaning: Name of an ancient teacher (a variant of the sage Galava)
golava.say_note: Three open syllables, phonetic from the spelling
golava.collisions: Essentially unused today; not to be confused with Galav
golava.note: A sage's name from the Puranas; the 'Golu' nickname is affectionate in Marathi households

gaulya.why_not: Means 'sweet-tasting' — a flavor adjective, too trivial for a name

chakas.name: Chakas
chakas.say_note: Clear consonants, though some may say 'CHAY-kas' at first
chakas.collisions: No name collisions; distinct from the common Chakshu
chakas.note: A grammarians' form meaning 'shining'; unusual but with a solid, positive sense

chanda.why_not: Reads as the feminine name Chanda/Chandaa; also 'chanda' means fierce/violent

chilli.why_not: Reads as the English word 'chilli'; guaranteed teasing

china.why_not: Identical to the country name in English

chuta.why_not: Sounds like crude slang in Hindi/Marathi; unusable

jajja.why_not: Doubled -jj- reads as a nonsense sound in English; uncertain etymology

jaloka.name: Jaloka
jaloka.meaning: Name of a king of Kashmir, son of Ashoka, in the Rajatarangini
jaloka.say_note: Fully phonetic; the stressed 'LOH' makes it easy
jaloka.collisions: Vanishingly rare as a modern name
jaloka.note: Historical royal name from Kalhana's chronicle; distinctive without sounding invented

java.why_not: Reads as Java the island/coffee/programming language despite the fine meaning 'swift'

javin.name: Javin
javin.say_note: Reads exactly as spelled; rhymes with Gavin, so Americans get it instantly.
javin.collisions: Echoes Gavin; occasionally seen as a modern Indian coinage but still rare.
javin.note: Vedic word for swiftness; crisp, two syllables, pairs cleanly with Gawande.

jahu.why_not: Means 'a young animal'; thin, odd meaning and reads like a laugh/interjection.

jajali.why_not: Three-syllable repeating 'ja-ja' sounds comic in English and invites teasing.

jalaka.why_not: Obscure tree name with a diminutive -ka ending; reads feminine in English.

jira.why_not: Identical to jeera, the Indian word for cumin — instant food joke in the community.

jiri.why_not: Reads feminine and clashes with Czech Jiří; also a Nepali place name.

jivin.name: Jivin
jivin.meaning: living, full of life; one who lives (in a certain way)
jivin.say_note: No aspirates or retroflexes; 'Jee-vin' is unambiguous from the spelling.
jivin.collisions: Close in sound to the common Jeevan, but the -in ending keeps it distinct.
jivin.note: Rooted in jīv, 'to live'; warm meaning, easy for American teachers.

jurni.why_not: Reads as English 'journey' misspelled; awkward consonant cluster.

jenya.name: Jenya
jenya.say_note: Simple JEN-yuh; the -nya glide is easy for Americans (cf. Sonya, Kenya-adjacent).
jenya.collisions: Shares sound with the Russian nickname Zhenya, which can read unisex.
jenya.note: Rigvedic word cognate with Greek gennaios; distinguished meaning, but parents should be fine with the Zhenya echo.

jnata.why_not: Initial jñ- cluster is unpronounceable for Americans and it is a participle, not a name.

jneya.why_not: jñ- cluster; also a pure grammatical gerundive ('to be known').

jmaya.why_not: Jm- cluster is unsayable in English and the meaning ('going on the earth') is flat.

jmayat.why_not: Unpronounceable cluster and a participial form, not a name.

jyayas.why_not: Comparative grammatical form ending in -as; hard to say and not name-like.

jvala.why_not: jv- cluster is mangled by Americans and Jwala is widely read as a girl's name.

takya.why_not: Reads as English 'tacky'; a gerundive form, not usable.

takva.why_not: kv cluster is clumsy in English and the word is a bare Vedic adjective.

tarda.why_not: A bird species name that reads like 'tardy'/worse in English.

tavya.name: Tavya
tavya.say_note: Two clean syllables, no aspirates; the -vya glide is manageable (like 'Sonya' pattern).
tavya.collisions: Slight echo of the girls' name Tanvya; otherwise unused.
tavya.note: Rigvedic adjective from the root tu, 'to be strong'; genuinely unused as a given name.

tayin.name: Tayin
tayin.meaning: protector, one who shelters (an epithet of the Buddha and Mahavira)
tayin.say_note: Phonetically transparent: TAH-yin, no clusters, no retroflex.
tayin.collisions: Resembles the Arabic-influenced Tayyib only loosely; not in use among Indian-Americans.
tayin.note: Buddhist/Jain epithet meaning protector; noble sense, very easy in an American classroom.

tima.why_not: Means a whale and reads as 'timid'/Tima-the-girl; weak.

tila.why_not: Means sesame seed — a kitchen word, and reads feminine.

tungaka.why_not: Place name with -ka ending; three syllables that Americans would stress wrongly.

tumra.why_not: 'Big, fat' connotation plus an mr cluster; reads like 'tumor'.

tura.why_not: Americans read it as 'tour-a'; also a girls'/place name elsewhere.

tulaji.why_not: A specific 18th-century Tanjore king; South-Indian-associated and dated.

tuta.why_not: Reads as 'tooter'/'tutu'; mulberry tree meaning is trivial.

tuya.why_not: Too slight; reads feminine and like Spanish 'tuya' (yours).

tripat.why_not: Ends in an English word 'pat' and reads as 'trip'; awkward despite the 'moon' sense.

taisha.why_not: Reads clearly as a girl's name in the USA (Taisha/Tayshia).

toka.why_not: Means the young of an animal; also reads as 'toker' slang.

tokman.why_not: Ends in '-man' as an English word and means malt/barley shoot; odd.

todana.why_not: Root tud- means 'to pierce/goad'; obscure tree, and it sounds feminine.

tratri.why_not: tr-tr consonant sequence is very hard for Americans; agent-noun form.

dava.why_not: Means a forest fire (destructive); also reads like 'Dava/Diva'.

datva.why_not: tv cluster is awkward in English; lexicographers' word only.

daman.name: Daman
daman.say_note: Two easy syllables; stress the first (DAH-mun) so it does not sound like 'demon'.
daman.collisions: Daman is also a coastal Indian town and a Punjabi/Sikh unisex name; not common among US Indian babies.
daman.note: Vedic word for a bestower; dignified, and the -an ending is not the trendy -aan style.

dasanu.why_not: Obscure semi-divine being; reads oddly, 'anu' ending weak and unclear meaning

dahin.why_not: Means 'burning'; negative, and reads like Hindi 'dahin' (right/curd-like)

didyut.why_not: Awkward consonant-final form, Americans would mangle it; sounds like a stammer

dilipa.why_not: Too close to Dilip, a very common older-generation Indian man's name

divya.why_not: Divya is overwhelmingly a girl's name in India and the diaspora

dishya.name: Dishya
dishya.meaning: Belonging to the horizons; of all directions of the sky
dishya.note: Fresh sky-themed word; pairs cleanly with Gawande

dipa.why_not: Reads as Deepa/Deepak, a common girl's name and older-generation base

dura.why_not: Reads as Hindi 'dur' (far/away) and feminine-sounding; ambiguous etymology

duloka.why_not: Just a poet's name; 'du-' prefix suggests 'bad' in Sanskrit, poor meaning

dutaka.why_not: Means forest conflagration/messenger-diminutive; awkward and negative

dupra.why_not: Lexicon-only word, sounds like 'duper'; bad English echo

driti.why_not: Means leather bag/bellows; weak meaning and feminine sound

dripra.why_not: Unpronounceable cluster for Americans; obscure lexicon word

devri.why_not: Means husband's brother — a kinship term, not a name

dyuga.why_not: Initial 'dy-' cluster is mangled by Americans ('dye-yuga'); odd sound

dyuvan.why_not: 'Dy-' onset unpronounceable from spelling; also reads like 'Yuvan' variant

dyutat.why_not: Participial grammatical form; harsh and unnameable

dyota.why_not: 'Dyota' is misread as 'dye-OH-ta'; awkward onset despite good meaning

drapsa.why_not: Means a drop (incl. semen); harsh cluster and poor connotation

dravat.name: Dravat
dravat.say_note: Reads straightforwardly; no aspirates or retroflex issues

dravya.why_not: Commonly means 'substance/wealth/material'; sounds like a mispronunciation of Dravya/Divya, feminine-leaning

nada.why_not: Reads as Spanish 'nada' (nothing) and is a girl's name in Arabic

napat.why_not: Reads as 'nap at'; bad English echo

nalina.name: Nalin
nalina.say_note: Simple, phonetic; final -a dropped as is standard for boys
nalina.collisions: Nalin exists as a name but is uncommon now; Nalini is the feminine
nalina.note: Clean lotus name, rare among US-born Indian kids

nava.why_not: Reads as a car brand/place and as 'Nova'; too thin as a name

nakoka.why_not: Just a poet's name; sounds comic/reduplicative in English

niruj.name: Niruj
niruj.collisions: Slight echo of Neeraj, an older-generation name
niruj.note: Strong wellbeing meaning; distinct but Neeraj adjacency is the one caveat

nigu.why_not: Lexicon-only, two-syllable oddity; sounds incomplete and slangy

nicha.why_not: 'Nicha' means low/base in Sanskrit and Hindi — strongly negative

niva.why_not: Reads as a feminine name/car brand (Niva/Nivea); weak meaning

nemita.why_not: Ends in -ita, reads feminine in American ears

naimba.why_not: Merely 'relating to the neem tree'; adjectival and odd-sounding

pajoka.why_not: Obscure poet's name; sounds like a joke word in English

pati.why_not: Means husband/lord; reads as English 'patty' and as the name Patty

padi.why_not: Uncertain meaning ('a kind of animal'); reads as 'paddy'

para.why_not: Reads as the English prefix 'para'; too generic as a standalone name

parda.why_not: Meaning is breaking wind; absolutely unusable

patri.why_not: Reads like English 'pastry'/'patry' and is a bare agent-noun stem; invites mangling.

paka.why_not: Means 'very young/cooking'; also reads as English slang and near 'Paka/Pak'; weak meaning.

patu.name: Patu
patu.say_note: Two clean open syllables; Americans read it correctly at sight.
patu.collisions: Distinct from the adjective 'patu' (clever); no common-name clash.
patu.note: Very short and unused; the 'Pat' nickname is the main thing to weigh.

pada.why_not: Means 'foot'; weak meaning and reads oddly in English.

payu.name: Payu
payu.meaning: A guard, a protector (Rigvedic word for helpful protecting powers)
payu.say_note: Simple CV-CV; no cluster or retroflex.
payu.collisions: No popular Indian-American name; unrelated to 'Piyu'.
payu.note: A homonym pAyu also means 'anus' in anatomical texts — worth flagging to the parents.

parshna.why_not: Obscure teacher's name with an rsh-n cluster Americans cannot say; also means 'heel'.

pali.why_not: Reads as the Pali language and as the common Punjabi nickname 'Pali'; not distinctive.

pavaki.name: Pavaki
pavaki.meaning: Son of Agni (fire) — an epithet of Skanda/Kartikeya
pavaki.say_note: All open syllables; spelled phonetically for English readers.
pavaki.collisions: Echoes 'Pavak', which is uncommon; -i ending may read slightly soft to some.
pavaki.note: Strong mythological anchor with essentially no usage today.

pikka.why_not: Means a young elephant; reads like 'picker/Pikachu' and is a lexicon curiosity.

piyaka.why_not: Obscure poet's name with no clear meaning; sounds like a diminutive.

pilu.why_not: Reads as 'pee-loo'; a shrub name and a common Bengali pet-name, not a strong given name.

piluka.why_not: Diminutive of a tree name; sounds like a nickname, not a name.

puroka.why_not: Meaning is uncertain even in the dictionary ('town-dweller?'); no defensible sense.

posha.name: Posha
posha.say_note: 'Po' + 'sha' — read correctly on first try by English speakers.
posha.collisions: Related word 'Poshan' is a noun, not a name; no popularity issue.
posha.note: 'Posh' as a nickname reads positive in American English.

paunya.why_not: Spelling invites 'pawn-ya'; a Vedic derivative form, and too close to 'Punya'.

pausha.name: Pausha
pausha.meaning: The winter month Pausha, when the full moon stands in the Pushya asterism
pausha.say_note: 'Pau' may be read as 'paw' or 'pow'; both are acceptable and close.
pausha.collisions: Recognizable to Indians as a month name rather than a personal name.
pausha.note: Good if the boy has a Pausha/Pushya birth link; otherwise it reads calendrical.

pyana.why_not: Unpronounceable initial cluster for Americans; obscure lexical word for 'sea'.

pradana.name: Pradan
pradana.say_note: Dropping the final -a gives a clean masculine two-syllable form.
pradana.collisions: Sounds near 'Pradhan' (a surname/title) — the spelling without h keeps it distinct.
pradana.note: 'Dan' is a natural American-friendly short form.

pramud.why_not: Too close to Pramod, a very common name for Indian men born 1950–1990.

prashu.why_not: Meaning uncertain ('eater, guest?'); also reads as the nickname for Prashant.

praha.why_not: Reads as the city Praha (Prague); the meaning 'instruction in dancing' is odd for a name.

priya.why_not: Overwhelmingly a girl's name in Indian and Indian-American usage.

bandin.why_not: Homophonous with 'bandi/bandhan' (captive, bound) and reads as 'bandit' to American ears.

bahavi.why_not: A patronymic form; the -vi ending reads feminine in American English.

bija.name: Bija
bija.meaning: Seed — the origin or germ of all growth (also the citron tree)
bija.say_note: Read correctly from the spelling; no cluster, no aspirate.
bija.collisions: A common noun in Marathi/Hindi, so it will read as 'seed' to Indian relatives.
bija.note: Clean, modern-sounding, and genuinely unused as a given name.
